utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. And welcome back after I think a six-week break in this trial. May we begin with taking the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution. And welcome back to the peaceful trial, to Judges Hall and Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Deirdre Montgomery appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Lennart Poulsen, and Miroslav Cuskic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We have been alerted that before we invite Mr. Krgovic to open, that there are a number of housekeeping matters. I don't know who wishes to go first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours can I deal with the ones that we notified Ms. Featherstone of, the one which was on our general e-mail Your Honour, first of all, Your Honours ordered us to disclose various documents in connection with the Zupljanin witness list under Rule 66(B). Your Honours, we have disclosed in respect of all witnesses except, and I don't believe protective measures were asked for -- no. I see Mr. Krgovic shaking his head. Krnjajic. Your Honours, he's very low on their list. There is a possibility, I understand, that he may not be available. I spoke to Mr. Krgovic about that, and he's happy to wait until he confirms that he will be called as a witness. The reason for that is that it's a very large search. Or a large number of documents, I should say. And Mr. Buhovac who is in fact the witness they wish to, or are calling under the terms of Rule 92 quater. He's actually dead. We just haven't had the opportunity to go through the search. So, Your Honour, that's the first matter. The second matter is -- relates to admission of documents. Your Honour, there's a translation that's been floating around the place. I wonder if Mr. Smith can bring it up. It is D89 -- 2D89, sorry. It's on Sanction, I gather. Now, Your Honour may recall this document. It was the one that was -- said to be illegible, first of all. Then Mr. Krgovic sent it back for CLSS who said it was illegible. We sent it back to CLSS who said, no, they couldn't decipher more and produced this translation. And since then we have applied once before to have this translation replace the original. There's been an objection Mr. Krgovic, but there has to come a time, particularly now we're on his case, where we say unless there's anything further coming from them, this translation should now be admitted and replace the one that is presently in e-court. So Your Honours, can I leave -- hear what Mr. Krgovic has to say before I move on to the second matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Ms. Korner is right. I had the document translated and even made a draft translation myself in order to assist the translation service. But the translation was returned when I wanted to use it and that's why this document was not admitted. When the Prosecution had the document retranslated they received a better translation than the Defence, and that was my objection. If I remember correctly, when we discussed this document, the last thing was that the Registry should apply for a retranslation. The translation service was to verify the translation or retranslate it. Since that time we've had no additional information. If we should be informed by the translation service that no better translation than that received by the Prosecution can be provided, I do not object to the old translation by this new one being replaced. But I think that we should wait for the reply of the translation service to the effect that no better translation with be made.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have no recollection of the Registry having anything to do with this at all. This translation is, by the way, a CLSS translation, not an OTP one. I don't know whether that -- the Registrar can help at all on this. But I have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Court Officer reports that because the parties are usually responsible for this, it wasn't a matter that came through her. But in terms of Mr. Korner's last point, about this being a CLSS translation, does that suffice your -- in terms of your reservations, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as far as I remember, the problem was the following: I requested the assistance of the Registry in this matter for a retranslation to be made because I think that it is possible to do. It is possible to get a better translation than the one made by CLSS upon the request of the OTP. I think that the quality of the translation is such that a higher quality translation certainly must be possible. That was -- these are my reservations. Because the Serbian version and the English version do not match.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is a fuller translation than the original on any showing. I'm quite happy if Mr. Krgovic can persuade CLSS to translate more of it and they come up with an even better version than we should replace that. But, at the moment I am anxious that this version which does contain more information should be the one that if it is used comes up in e-court. So may I ask that Your Honours order that the replacement take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I would suggest is that, rather than acceding to that request immediately, that perhaps both sides speak out of court over the next day or two and consult whomever else they need to over at CLSS or others, and come back and one of could report later in the week, say, the day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours, I'm very happy to -- this has now dragged on for months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's why I said the day after tomorrow. I'm not suggesting an interminable discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... speak out of court and come back and let us know where we are in two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honours I'm perfectly happy to see if Mr. Krgovic or both of us together can persuade CLSS to have another look at it. The second matter relating to admission of exhibits is, over the adjournment I noticed, when I was checking, that we seem to have admitted some of the ethnic maps that are in the booklet but not all of them for some unknown reason. My application is now can we simply make that the whole book of ethnic maps a single exhibit? With the divisions therein. In other words -- I've forgotten where we got up in Prosecution exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It may be my imagination but I seem to recall about three months ago this question coming up, and I being corrected by, I think, both sides in my impression that the whole book had been in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's what -- I must say I was under that impression. It may well be that I said that. But when we checked the list of exhibits, Mr. Smith discovered that some had been individually admitted and others hadn't been. And there doesn't seem to be any rhyme or reason, as I think all of them were shown to a particular witness and I don't know -- sorry, not all of them were shown to a particular witness. They were all shown to a different witness who came from particular municipalities. So can I ask: If we're right, and I'm sure the Registry will correct us if we're wrong, that 65 ter 10236. -- from .02 to .15 be made a court exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Zecevic had sprung to his feet when you first lit on this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... let me see what he has so say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I seem to recall Ms. Korner protesting when she wasn't put on notice about the issues that were raised by the Defence. In this case, we were not put on notice that she is going to request the admittance of these documents. Therefore I suggest that we postpone the decision until we discuss that and get to know the matter because I -- from my recollection I cannot really, honestly say at this point what is -- what was the position and what happened and why wasn't that admitted. Therefore, I suggest that we discuss that over the break, and then inform the Trial Chamber. Thank you. Basically, I'm objecting to this at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Quite right, I'm sorry. It didn't occur to me that there was going to be any problems so I'm perfectly happy to leave it until after the break and talk to Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Krgovic about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are just two other matters which may be looking a little far ahead but not that far ahead, possibly. Firstly, Your Honour, can I just raise for Your Honours to consider, having been watching and listening to the Haradinaj trial last Friday, I noted that there was some suggestion, certainly from the Defence that there was insufficient evidence to fill the full two weeks that had been allotted to them after we finished this three-week period n which case, it was -- it was a question of whether there should be evidence available for us to take up the extra week as, indeed, I heard Mr. Emmerson suggesting. But I simple raise that for Your Honours to consider. Second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may respond briefly to a portion of that, I don't know if you were able -- whether you got what the court said after it took a brief break on Friday, but, as far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, we -- as presently advised we see the whole next three-week slot being fully utilized.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the Haradinaj case. I think it's two weeks. We're going from three weeks to two, alternating two weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, the next slotted period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Your Honours. Then can I come to the question of the final trial brief. I don't expect an answer at this stage, but to merely inquire of Your Honours or to ask Your Honours to consider how long you would give from the conclusion of the evidence to the filing, for the filing of these briefs, and obviously we would be asking for more -- a larger page allowance than is the standard one, given the length of trial, the amount of evidence and two accused. So I'm just putting that out for consideration. And finally, Your Honours, I know Your Honours Mr. Hannis has mentioned this before and we're not asking for information, but obviously if Your Honours were considering calling witnesses yourselves, then it would be useful to know as soon as Your Honours felt able whether you were, how many, and if I can point out, it's -- certain witnesses will need or certain persons that Your Honours may be considering may need considerable arrangements to be made, just so that we have that there. And, Your Honour, those are the matters that I wish to raise this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are there any other matters before Mr. Krgovic begins?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Briefly, I informed Ms. Featherstone about the three matters that I wished to raise. One matter is, Your Honours will recall that one of the witnesses, Mr. Dragan Andan, was required by the Trial Chamber to produce a certain document which was in his collection, in his possession back home. And after that, we didn't have any -- any information about it. During the break, I contacted Mr. Andan, and he informed me that two days after his return back home he contacted VWS and provided the document to the VWS. I informed him that we had no knowledge whatsoever, that we never got any information from VWS about the arrival of that document, and then he informed me that he personally contacted the persons in Sarajevo about that document, and they confirmed that the document, which they received from him, according to the -- to the Chamber's orders, was sent to The Hague. And that is the information that I got. Now, at this point, if Your Honours will -- would -- would require from me to -- to investigate the matter with the VWS or approach VWS about the document, I will gladly do so. I just didn't want to do that on my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you for your offer, Mr. Zecevic. The first method would probably be to ask the Court Officer to see what investigations, what her investigations will -- might reveal. And ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So in the -- hopefully in the course of today we will have a report as to where that errant document may be. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The second matter, I believe we would need to go to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Private, I'm sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, are you ready to open?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to the indictment drafted by the Prosecution, my client, Stojan Zupljanin, is being charged with serious crimes, punishable under the Statute of this Tribunal. When we were considering how to put up our Defence, we decided to call a limited number of witnesses. They were to testify about certain events, as well as the conduct and the acts of Stojan Zupljanin. During the OTP case, we were all faced with a great number of facts. If they are looked upon from one side only, they will not assist you in determining the truth. You will have to consider the wider context of the genesis and development of a dramatic situation that led to the breakup of a country, a tragic war, a lot of suffering, and, unfortunately, many crimes. That is why, during the Defence case, the Defence will insist on certain concepts, which, to our mind, will greatly assist you in understanding the facts fully and drawing founded conclusions. One of these concepts the Defence will dwell upon during the Defence case is context. Facts taken out of context can only give rise to false conclusions and -- and lead the trier of fact to wrong conclusions. We will call a number of witnesses who were immediate participants in the events who have first-hand knowledge about the most relevant facts from the indictment. But, at the same time, they are witnesses who have knowledge about the overall context in which there were very complicated relationships. These relationships existed at various levels, and we mustn't disregard them. They existed in the international community too, and are reflected in its attitude toward the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. These relationships existed among the participants in the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina too. In order to understand the position and the criminal liability of Stojan Zupljanin, it is imperative to consider this context and assess his ability to act under these circumstances and take such actions as he was empowered to do under the law. At the moment, when the conflict in the Autonomous Region of Krajina began, there were many armed people, there were armed groups of various ethnicities. At that moment, the Banja Luka CSB had only 2.000 police officers, active police officers; and, by the end of 1992, some 5.000 reserve police officers. I'm talking about a territory inhabited by about a million people. 80 per cent of all these police officers were used in combat activities, where they were no longer under the control of Mr. Zupljanin. That is the context that the witnesses will talk about and give evidence. What is characteristic and has been pointed out by Mr. Zupljanin while the Prosecution witnesses were being examined is the following: Throughout the period covered by the indictment, there were combat activities in a part of the territory. There were organised extremist groups and other armed groups, whose goal it was to undermine the constitutional order and security. They were planning to carry out sabotage and terrorist activities aimed at the population and facilities. They planned and executed such actions. They were illegally armed. And armed groups consisting of Muslim and Croatian extremists were active there were disruptions of public law and order, there were armed attacks on the members of the security forces, and what is most important, Your Honour, from the aspect of policing, was a disregard for the law. There was also wide-spread civil disobedience at that time. There was a lower level of social tolerance, and there was a rise in the number of the most serious crimes, such as banditism, causing general danger, and there was general insecurity, as well as poverty that became ever more wide-spread. All these are the elements that made up the context in which Stojan Zupljanin had to act. What I can point out as another problem in the territory of the CSB is -- are the criminal activities of armed groups and individuals of Serbian ethnicity. Such a way of operating by those groups created mistrust in the work of the police and a feeling of lack of safety. On top of that, many of the perpetrators bore the insignia of the police and the army. On the other hand, a lack of efficiency and professionalism in a number of public security stations, as well as their de facto independence of the centre, led to such a situation in which the work of the police was the way we could see. Your Honours, this last topic I covered can be found in Stojan Zupljanin's report, which he submitted at the end of every year to the Ministry of Interior. This Defence will show, within that context, that everything Mr. Stojan -- Stojan Zupljanin did was aimed at preventing or at least alleviating the consequences of such a state of affairs. Now to what extent he was successful in doing so is a different matter. However, Stojan Zupljanin cannot be held responsible for perhaps not being completely up to the task, although he need not necessarily agree with me. It is not a war crime to be less than a good chief. In order to corroborate its assertions I have just discussed, this Defence will also lead a military expert. He will try to explain to the Bench what the nature and circumstances of the work of the police was in -- at the time of war; the war being the one in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1992. All this was part of the general background needed to view, to discuss the role of the army and the mutual relationships between the army and the police in the execution of combat activities, as well as implementing military tasks by the police. You will have before you a number of policemen from the Banja Luka CSB who worked alongside Stojan Zupljanin in 1992. They were also participants in a number of specific events. Among them, there will be a number of Muslims and Croats. The Defence will also lead evidence on the activities and establishment of special units in the area of the Autonomous Region of the Krajina, as well as on the scope of their authority, liability, and mutual relationships. These witnesses will try to discuss some of the facts covered by the various OTP witnesses in more detail. The Defence will also put forth as witnesses a number of participants in the war-affected area, including Prijedor, Kotor Varos, Kljuc, Sanski Most, and these people will speak from their point of view about certain events which have been discussed here. We will also have a number of employees of the CSB appear as witnesses who held different positions in the CSB. The testimony of such witnesses led by the Defence will, in a way, serve as an addition to the evidence heard by the Court thus far, in order to further shed light on the acts and conduct of Stojan Zupljanin. To conclude, Your Honours, this Defence submitted a number of statements aimed at drawing a picture of Stojan Zupljanin as a person, provided by Stojan Zupljanin's co-citizens and people who used to work with him. In keeping with your decision, you will also hear some of that evidence led in the courtroom. Those people will talk about Stojan Zupljanin's personality and his actions in 1992. Having in mind all OTP evidence and the evidence provided by Mico Stanisic's Defence, as I have explained already, we opted for a limited number of witnesses, in order to address specific circumstances and events in an attempt at drawing the context of these events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In this way, we hope to assist the Chamber in finally reaching the fair -- a fair decision. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I just mention one matter and I think it was a slip of the tongue by Mr. Krgovic page 13, line 7, he said, "What is characteristic and has been pointed out by Mr. Zupljanin ..." I'm assuming he meant Mr. Zupljanin' Defence. I wonder if he could just correct that because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll say it again. I understand there was no translation. Mr. Krgovic said at page 13, line 7: "What is characteristic and has been pointed out by Mr. Zupljanin ..." What he meant, and I see he agrees is the Defence of Mr. Zupljanin, because of course Mr. Zupljanin hasn't pointed anything out at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, I assume your witness is available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Could we proceed now or maybe we can have a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If this is an urgent need for a break of course we would accommodate you. I just wondered why, because it is always better to stick to the established pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, there is no problem. I simply wanted to be forthcoming and assist the Chamber and the other participants in the proceedings. In any case, I'm fully prepared to go ahead immediately, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, while the witness is on his way in, the -- we were wondering whether we were -- whether there was a misprint in the communication that we received, that you expected that you would spend 20 hours in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, Your Honours it is not. Your Honours, this is the only military expert that the Defence are calling. Your Honours, I have a large number of issues I wish to deal with him, and a large number of documents which may not be covered by him, but certainly -- or not covered by him in his report but which we say are relevant. Can I say it is an excessive caution. Normally, I underestimate and end up having to ask Your Honours for more time, but nonetheless, as Your Honours will understand, the fact that Mr. Krgovic says he is only going to spend six hours is not the point. If you recall, we were given three hours with Mr. Nilsson and the Defence spent 13 hours with him. It's a difference of approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we should alert the witness that he will be with us well into next week. [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It may well be, and I hope [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As presently advised [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As presently advised, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Would you please read the solemn declaration on the card that the usher is now handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. And from your responses so far, I gather that you are in fact hearing me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we welcome you to the Tribunal and thank you for you're agreeing to assist by providing relevant evidence to us. I would, first of all, point out that the solemn declaration that you have just taken imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony and this Tribunal is empowered by the Statute that constituted it to impose penalties for perjury in terms of persons who give false or misleading testimony. You have been called by counsel representing the second accused in this matter, Mr. Zupljanin, and there are a number of preliminary questions the Bench would have of you before I invite Mr. Krgovic, who is lead counsel, to begin. Although we do have a copy of your report and annexed to it is your biography, would you, for the record, tell us your name, and your date of birth. The English translation that we have indicates your date of birth as the 2nd of August, 1995 which is, of course, an arithmetical impossibility. So perhaps you could also indicate to us your correct date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Mr. President, I was born on 2nd of August, 1955 [Realtime transcript read in error "1952"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Your name, sir, is ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Vidosav Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And what was your -- what is your present profession and/or the profession that occupied most of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of my life I was a professional soldier. Now I am a retired general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to take your report out of the bag that you have beside you. General, just one small correction for the transcript. I believe you said you were born on the 2nd of August, 1955. Whereas, in the transcript, we have 1952. Can you tell me whether I heard what you said correctly?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: You are correct. I said I was born on the 2nd of August, 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Krgovic. If you would take your seat for a moment. Mr. Kovacevic, there are one or two things that I forgot to mention before I invited Mr. Krgovic to begin. One is to remind you of the procedure whereby the side calling you begins. Counsel for the co-accused would have a right to also cross-examine you. And then counsel for the Prosecution would have their turn to cross-examination, and we return to Mr. Krgovic. Now, counsel have indicated that, between the times that they expect they would spend with you, that your testimony will extend throughout this week and well into next week. It may very well be that it doesn't take as long as that, and the times of sittings of the court if it's the -- because courtroom space has to be shared, it means that the morning sittings run from 9.00 to 1.45; afternoon sittings run from 2.15 to 7.00. But those sittings are not continuous. They are broken up into intervals of not more than 90 minutes, because largely for technical reasons in that the tapes that record these proceedings have to be changed. Now we -- our practice is a 20-minute break and that allows for the convenience and comfort for yourself and everyone else involved. But if at any point before a scheduled break, for instance it is 10.10 and the next scheduled break would be at 10.25 in about 15 minutes, but if, at any time, for whatever reason, you would require the Court to take a break before the scheduled break, please let us know and we will accommodate you. Thank you Mr. Krgovic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in your CV, I see you stated you were born in Liplje in the municipality of Kotor Varos in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did you ever reside in Kotor Varos itself?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, it is true I was born in the village of Liplje in the municipality of Kotor Varos. It is a village in wilderness but not very good for modern-day life. That is why in 1965 my parents moved to a town called Prnjavor, also in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In other words, I never lived in Kotor Varos. I can only add that in my native village -- rather, I returned to my native village for the first time after 20 years when I brought my wife and children to show them the place where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A question about the area you live in, or, rather, because of the area where you lived, did you ever meet Mr. Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I never met him personally, but I do know of his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you something, General. I am a fast talker, and it takes time to interpret what you and I say, as we share the same language. Could I ask you to pause briefly after my questions so as to avoid any overlaps in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in your CV, I can see that you attended the military high school and the air force academy and so on, following the completion of your primary schooling. I wanted to ask you this: Who was it that assigned you to serve in the army? What particular body.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When I completed primary school in Prnjavor, which is something I've already mentioned, I applied to -- I applied for education at the Military Academy, which was announced publicly. Following a medical exam in Belgrade, I was notified by the then-Secretariat for All People's Defence and contacted by the defence secretariat in Prnjavor, in order to have me enlisted into the military schools in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, we can see what schools you completed. Could you explain in more detail the education you gained at the air force academy and the officers' course. What type of schools were these and what qualifications you gained in those schools prior to the breakout of the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The military air force academy -- or, rather, I should put it this way. Having graduated from the air force academy in Belgrade, in Serbia --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, having graduated from the military secondary school in Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to the air force academy. When I completed the air force academy, which included basic military studies, I was assigned the first officer's rank which is of lieutenant. As such, one can command a platoon as a basic military unit. Upon completion of the Military Academy, I was transferred to serve in the Pula garrison in the Republic of Croatia. From there, I was sent to attend a course for air force officers for guiding air-strikes. Having completed that course, I returned to my unit as a fully qualified officer in that area. I was supposed to act as part of the anti-aircraft defence system. Having spent three years in the Pula garrison where I successfully completed my duties, I was transferred to a battalion, which is the next higher-ranking unit. I was also assigned to a more senior position. I acted as assistant battalion commander in charge of political affairs and education, as it was called at the time. It took place in 1980. In the Republic of Slovenia, which is where the battalion was located, I spent three years. In 1983, I was again transferred to the regiment command in charge of air force reconnaissance, which was in Zagreb in Croatia. Prior to that date, I had married, and we had our first child, our daughter, in Pula. My next child, a son, was born in Slovenia. This means that I arrived in Zagreb with my entire family. In Zagreb, a few years later, having been a successful officer, I was transferred to the political school of the Yugoslav People's Army, which was a school at tactical level. And it was one of the conditions to be further promoted to higher ranks and being placed in more senior positions. Unfortunately, I did not complete that school. The duration of that training was two years. The reason was the fact that, in 1991, the civil war broke out. In other words, armed conflict began in the Republic of Slovenia, and I think it was about the 25th of June, 1991 when all training, officers' training, was broken off, and we all had to return to our respective units. Now, to sum up and answer your question, until the beginning of the war, I was mostly active in moral guidance of soldiers and officers. I taught, I visited units to have briefings there and work with people. At the time, there were no psychologists in the Yugoslav People's Army. There weren't any priests or ministers either. Those who were active in moral guidance were the only ones to work with people, to counsel them, and educate them. Apart from that, my responsibility comprised co-operation with the local population. That is, having contacts with municipal leaderships, the MUP, the veterans' organisations, the church, media, and the like. On top of all that, any officer with a certain position and status in a command was a member or a chief of the operative duty team, the task of which was to be in charge of all matters during the absence of the commander, because those units never ceased to operate. This would be the briefest possible summary of my activities and responsibilities until the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is this a convenient point, Mr. Krgovic? So -- so we take our first break and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you briefly described your activities before the war, and you mentioned that you were chief of the operative duty team. Could you briefly explain what that is?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The command of the regiment where I worked had two air guidance and surveillance battalions, which, in turn, comprised a number of lower-ranking units; namely, air guidance and surveillance companies. Their basic work tools were air surveillance radars. The regiment command had its units in three of the then-republics. That is, Croatia, Slovenia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those radars enabled us to have an image of air-space in that zone of responsibility covering the three republics I mentioned, as well as the frontiers and all air traffic in Yugoslav air-space. The information flow was toward the operation centres. They were underground, and these facilities were of strategic importance for national defence. The duty teams were located there. Every aircraft in air-space had a certain designation. Civilian aircraft were marked C; whereas, military aircraft were marked Y; whereas, unidentified or enemy aircraft were marked X. When an unidentified or enemy aircraft appeared unannounced and did not travel in the air traffic corridors for civilian air traffic, we would alarm our units. There were fighter aircraft on duty at our air strips, and there were also units on duty in our anti-aircraft missile units. All these units would have their combat readiness raised by one level, and the operative duty teams were the ones who decided about the use of these units. Clearly, those teams were much stronger in the army commands. The most important team was the operative duty team of the General Staff of the army. It controlled all activities of the units at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, let me follow up on your last sentence. You mentioned in your biography, or, rather, your CV that you're also assistant commander for political guidance and the chief of the morale section in the Army of Serbia and Montenegro. Were you -- were you chief of that operative duty team at the level of the entire armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That operative duty team is headed by a general who completed the highest level army schools, such as the National Defence School. Those were the conditions that had to be fulfilled. I personally headed the operative duty team of the General Staff of the then-army two or three times a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to your qualifications and training, were you qualified to command the Army of Yugoslavia as the -- as chief of the operative duty team?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That was our duty at all hours, when the chief of General Staff was not at his workplace. That team consisted of about a dozen men who were specialists for the branches. That is, the army, air force, navy, or infantry, et cetera. It is a known fact that the one trained to decide about the use of the air force as one of the most complex system in any army can also make decisions about the use of other systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To be able to do that, did you have to have a -- have an in-depth knowledge of the army and any other branches of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, in order to be chief of the operative duty team?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The schools I completed after the war included the Command Staff Academy of the Land Army. That was a coincidence. I was unable to continue to attend the political school of the JNA where I had enrolled before the war, because that school was abolished. In 2001 or 2002, I completed the highest school in the armed forces, and that's the General Staff College, which is a school for all branch services. All types of operations are dealt with there, all the -- on land, in the air, and at sea. Certainly everybody focussed on matters that were more closely linked to their actual activities. But you also had to know about matters concerning other branches or combat arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned the Command Staff Academy of the Land Army and you said that graduated from that school in 1994. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I skipped part of your CV because I wanted to clarify what the operative duty team did, and its chief included. What was your position, sir, when the conflict in Slovenia began? That is the armed conflict in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I was assistant regiment commander for political guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I see in your CV when you mention wartime service. Please give us additional information about your responsibilities and positions during the war, or your wartime experience, if you will?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I have already mentioned that the regiment command was responsible for three republics, because that's where its units were, these air surveillance and guidance companies and radar stations. When the armed conflict in Slovenia broke out, it was very easy to block these units. In peacetime, the food supply and fuel supply, as well as the supply of ammunition and spare parts was on a weekly or biweekly or monthly basis. All these units were located in mountainous areas. There was only one access road to their positions so that, at the beginning of the armed conflicts in Slovenia, all our units were soon blocked by the Slovenian TO. They ran out of food, water, and other supplies. Officers of Slovenian ethnicity, as well as the rank and file, started deserting JNA units from day one, and they went over to the TO. An unusual incident was recorded. The deputy battalion commander, our battalion in Slovenia, that is, the number-two man, deserted the JNA, joined the TO, and, only one day later, he led that TO unit in the attack on his own unit that he had commanded until the previous day. The unit was commanded by a young officer who was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I apologise. I see the Prosecutor is on her feet. I was asking you about your experience and wasn't trying to elicit such detailed information. I was only interested in essential information about any operations and whether you took part in any military operations on the ground because we are focussed on the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So if you could just briefly tell us what your position was, whether you were in the trenches, whether you took part in part in any deblocking situations and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, sir. To put it briefly, it was the regiment command's task - and when I say "regiment command," that includes me - to try to assist those units and those men who were -- were sealed off by supplying them with the basic necessities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally take part in the unblocking of those units and pulling them out to Croatia and then onto Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the war, the regiment command had about 35 staff. At the end, only four or five officers remained so that we did everything that had to be done, irrespective of our original duties. Since the Pleso air strip, where I was, was also blocked, we organised, or we put up a circular defence where I commanded the first defence section and I spent four to five hours in the trenches. Of course, I took part in the pulling out of our units from Slovenia. It was a real chaos, albeit small scale. Some people left their apartments behind; some left their families behind. They had to be persuaded that it was their first and foremost task to pull out our military materiel and equipment and then move on. I also personally took part in the operation when our units were pulled out from Pleso air strip and relocated to Bihac, where we arrived in late November 1991. I, and part of the command, stayed in Bihac until the 10th of May, 1992, I believe. Pursuant to a decision of the state leadership about the retreat or pullout of the units of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, we were transferred to Belgrade garrison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I can see from your CV that, in 1991 and in 1992, you served as the chief of the press centre of the 5th Corps of the Air Defence, and you were also assistant commander for morale guidance of the 5th Regiment. Tell me, please, which of these two positions was in Zagreb; and which one was in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Until my arrival in Bihac, I was officially assistant commander for morale, guidance and political affairs, as it was known at the time. In addition to that, I was -- I discharged the duties of the personnel organ and some other tasks. I told you that the regiment command was down to four or five officers. In addition to these duties, I was also the duty officer within the duty operations team which worked in the well-known underground facility in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, please, how many people did your unit have in the period when the conflict broke out in Slovenia; and with how many men did you arrive in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think that the regiment had some 600 to 700 people, and only one-third of them arrived in Bihac. Because after some time, there was a decision of the state leadership, stating that officers who were ethnic Slovenes and ethnic Croats could leave the JNA units, were allowed to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about when you arrived Bihac? What was the situation then? Were you able to move about freely, communicate? You, members of the JNA. Were you able to go and visit your family in Prnjavor? And also, what was the situation like with the soldiers an officers who were ethnic Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... before we deal with the General's answer. I did ask that if he was going to give evidence over and above what is contained in his report that I should be given notice of it. I have had no notice that he was going to be giving evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it wasn't my intention to go into these facts. However, in part of his report, the witness speaks about how the Army of Republika Srpska was established, how some officers and soldiers left, and so on. And in that report, he said that he wrote all that partially based on his personal experience and partially based on documents and so on. And that is the only purpose of this examination. I have no intention of going into details. I just wanted to explore the personal experience of this witness, how he left Slovenia, and how he arrived in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, firstly, can I be directed to the part of the report that Mr. Krgovic says this arises from. And, secondly, for the moment, I'll say nothing but it may mean that I need time to explore the issues that are being raised, about what happened when he arrived in Bihac. But, perhaps, first of all, you could tell you which part of the report this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's item 12, where the witness speaks about what he used, what part of his experience he relied on. And then in items 43, 44, 45, 47, 48, 49, 50, in all of these items or paragraphs, the witness speaks about the following apart of JNA, the creation of the VRS, and these are precisely the topics that I'm exploring with the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I say, I'm not, at the moment going to take the matter further but it is not good enough, we would submit, to say when all the the General says in paragraph 12: "I included elements of my personal experience ..." for this to be developed without notice of exactly what the personal experience is said to be. But, as I say, for the moment, I'll let this continue without further objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we came to this point. Now tell us, please, what was the situation? What was the situation like with the ethnic Muslims serving in the JNA? And what was the role of the JNA, what were the goals of the JNA that you were made aware of via orders, instructions, and so on, that you received from the superior command?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What I was able to see concerning the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was very complex. Roads were under blockade. The officers and soldiers who were Muslims had also started leaving the JNA. There was great animosity towards members of the JNA. As far as I'm aware, the then-task of the JNA, as far as we informed the people, was to keep the warring sides apart, keep them separate, to the greatest possible level. And also creating buffer zones. I personally think that the JNA did not have a proper goal and that this is precisely why it ended the way it did. Because the JNA did not succeed in fulfilling its mandate, its task, because the army itself was exposed to attacks by paramilitary and para-police forces in certain republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before you left Bihac, did you try via your own Secretariat for National Defence which had sent you to JNA originally to find some kind of a position in Bosnia-Herzegovina, given that your unit was in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that its further fate was uncertain?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a proper wartime nightmare and chaos. People didn't know what to do. The fate of the JNA was uncertain and unknown. Since I had been sent by the military department in Prnjavor to various military schools, I believed that I should go to my birth town while one was still able to move about. I think that it was in early January of 1992. I wanted to go there and to report, to sign up as an officer, because I knew that the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina would eventually break out. I wanted to present myself, to tell them what my credentials were, even though they were fully aware of it. It was necessary for them to write a request in order for me to be engaged. They were supposed to send the request to my then-command within the JNA, where I served. They didn't do that. The then-Serb leadership didn't really have much confidence, didn't really trust me as an officer of the JNA. They described all of us as Communist officers. That was the term they used for us. Therefore, I never received call-up papers from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you were pulling out from Bihac on your way to Belgrade in 1992, were you able to use regular roads or not? How did you carry out the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was an air evacuation, for the most part. As far as I can remember, the roads in Bosnia and Herzegovina were already cut off, and I think that there was an order of the President of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or of some minister, or perhaps the TO commander, from April, to that effect, one could conduct a land evacuation, but with previous notifications, permits, and similar type of paperwork which was quite ridiculous because the JNA was still the federal army and the official armed force. It was ridiculous, and it was humiliating. Whoever wanted, could have stopped you at a check-point, could have harassed you, questioned you, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, further on in your CV I can see that you served in certain posts in Belgrade. And then I see here that, from November 1995 until December - I think it is a mistake here, it should be 1996 - you served in the Army of Republika Srpska. Can you tell us briefly what positions did you hold and how you ended up going there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic keeps saying this is an mistake in the curriculum vitae. But the curriculum vitae I have a copy of says that, 1996. I'm just wondering what Mr. Krgovic is looking at and what I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the Serbian version. That's where the problem is. Let me just look at the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... upload the -- put onto the screen the two versions side by side. But -- in the English version I have got of the CV and that's why I'm wondering if it's the same one. It says that he served in the VRS between 1995 and 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another page that speaks of wartime service. It's page 3. There's a mistake there. From the 7th of November, 1995 until 14th of December, 1995. That's the mistake that I had in mind. Wartime service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question, General.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I was sent to Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the very end of the war, pursuant to an order of the General Staff of the then-army. I think that I was instructed to report to the Main Staff. That's what the order said, the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Since I served in the air force - that was my speciality - I went to the command of air force and anti-aircraft defence, which was located in Banja Luka, and reported to them. I expected that they would issue further assignments for me. As far as I'm aware, the air force command informed the Main Staff that I had arrived at their command, and I remained there until the end of 1996. As is well known, the war ended soon thereafter. It was in November 1995. Dayton Accords were signed so that I spent most of the time implementing the Dayton Agreement on the ground. As a liaison officer, I cooperated with the then-command ^ of the Multinational Division West, headed by General Jackson. In addition to that, since I was -- I had a position in the moral guidance, religious and legal affairs organ, I also had to solve all kinds of issues that were within the jurisdiction of that organ. It mostly had to do with providing information to the servicemen, assisting men in solving enormous post-war problems. Also providing assistance to the families of fallen soldiers, co-operation with the church authorities, the municipal authorities, and so on. I think I also took part in organising the first post-war elections in Banja Luka which were organised under the sponsorship of international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you described your duties, you spoke of co-operation with various parts of civilian authorities. Within the organ for morale guidance, were you also tasked with co-operating with civilian authorities? Could you tell us what civilian authorities those were and based on what did you co-operate with them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. The co-operation with civilian authorities, civilian organs on the ground, was part of my job description. However, it was conducted pursuant to a decision or pursuant to the consent of my commander, and also pursuant to the plan for co-operation which had its elements. It had content, it had designated persons who were supposed to carry it out, it defined the deadlines, it defined the territory and so on. So depending on the various plans, we carried out this co-operation. Sometimes we organised various ceremonies, celebrations. We cleared the ground. We did work on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To step back a bit, did you also co-operate with police organ during this period of time; and, if so, how did that co-operation develop?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not co-operate much with police organs on the ground. That was the task of the security officer in the command. Given that we had joint briefing every morning with the commander, I could hear their reports, and, thus, I know that they cooperated with them, that they exchanged the relevant information, and, as I have already told you, our facilities were of particular significance for the state, so they had special status. They were treated, they had special treatment, by the organs of the interior during peacetime. This now refers to the security and protection provided by them to these facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, just another area of your biography. You stated here that, in 1999, you also had wartime service during the NATO aggression on Yugoslavia. What was the post you occupied at the time?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think that I served in the organ for moral guidance of the air force and anti-air defence, and it was headquartered in Zemun, in Serbia. The greatest part of my activities and those of the entire organ focussed on informing the servicemen and undertaking measures to strengthen the combat morale. A large part of my time was devoted to gathering photo and video documentation about the destructive NATO attacks on our positions, as well as documentation concerning combat activities of our units. Therefore, I was frequently in the immediate vicinity of our rocket facilities, air force facilities, radar, and land army facilities, including naval forces in Montenegro that were subject to air-strikes. Also in situations where our forces engaged in counter-attacks. The material thus collected was used by me after the war when, together with several colleagues and experts from civilian establishment, I made a documentary about the participation of the units of air force during NATO aggression. This film is shown occasionally to the units to this day on the anniversary of those tragic events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can I have some usher's assistance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, as part of your duties, did you spend any time in Kosovo during the air campaign?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was the head of the team I discussed, which was in charge of collecting video and photographic material. Some 15 days prior to the end of the war, I found myself in Kosovo during the time of the aggression. This is where I awaited the withdrawal of our army from Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we're now so far removed from anything to do with this case. I know Your Honours are, no doubt, very interested in Kosovo in 1999 but I really do think we ought to get back to the subject of his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely tried to go through the witness's wartime experience briefly and through this part of his work. This was the last topic on his participation in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I see in your CV that you completed, in addition to the Command Staff Academy of the army, also the National Defence School in 2002. Can you tell us what is that school? What were you qualified to do, having completed that school? And what rank did you receive? Was this one of the prerequisites to further advance your career?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In Serbia, that school is the highest, the most senior level of military education. It is one of the preconditions in order to become a general, as the most senior rank in the armed forces. Military strategy is one of the subjects, operatics, tactics, command and control, as well as the methodology of military science. The courses taken as part of the curriculum enabled the officers to hold the most senior positions in the army, starting with that of a brigade commander, corps commander, to assistant commander of the General Staff, and chief of the General Staff. One can also hold certain positions within the Ministry of Defence. In any given class, there are about 30 officers who complete their studies, and only one, two, or three of the entire class make generals subsequently, depending on the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Following that, I can see that you were appointed chief of the National Defence School of the Army of Serbia and Montenegro. Is this the same school you discussed a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Following some organisational changes in the then-armed force, the morale administration no longer existed, and I had headed that administration within the General Staff. Instead, I was appointed chief of the National Defence School, the same school I had attended and completed in 2000, I think. Or 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, as far as I can tell from your CV, you also appear to have been chief of the Land Forces School in the Army of Serbia. Is this what we, as laymen, refer to as the Military Academy? And what was your role when you held that post?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my last professional position in the army. I held that position for four years. As part of the Military Academy or, in other words, under my command, there was also the military high school which I had completed back in 1974, as well as the School of National Defence, plus the basic military studies taught at the Military Academy. Together with my team, I created the project of unifying the entire military educational system under one roof. At first, some foreign colleagues of mine were confused by this concept, which is what I realized when I travelled abroad to Greece, Turkey, Italy, Russia. Despite that, they recognised the effort, believing it to be a rational approach for such a small country as Serbia. Together with my team, I succeeded for the first time in the history of the Military Academy, which is over 160 years old, to have the diplomas of the Military Academy awarded to the cadets upon graduation recognised as part of the civilian educational system in Serbia and, consequently, in all of Europe. We used the system of accreditation, and we also relied on the Bologna Declaration system in order to have the credits awarded and conditions met that would be necessary for such recognition. For the first time, girls were allowed to attend the Military Academy in Serbia, creating an opportunity for them to become officers. As we speak, the first female generation is graduating from the Military Academy, and they enrolled at the time when I was at the head of the academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, as someone who was at the helm of the Military Academy and someone who had graduated from the National Defence School, were you fully qualified to teach at the Military Academy?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Any officer who had graduated from the National Defence School, upon completing a specific didactic and methodology course which is also part of the school curriculum aimed at those teaching can teach the military subject in the curriculum such as military strategy, operatics, tactics, and command and control. Of course, in order to become a good lecturer, one needs to spend at least several years within the military educational system, in addition to having a very rich educational experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, in your report, you use a number of military terms, such as co-operation, attachment, and a number of other command and control military terms. Did you ever conduct or command exercises in practice when all such terms were used from the system of command and control as part of co-ordinated action?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I had such opportunity as part of the duty operations teams, as well as the head of the Military Academy, because, at the end of each year, the cadets graduating that year undergo a tactical exercise comprising cadets of all arms and branches, and live ammunition is used. Such exercises include over 1.000 participants, and there is co-ordination between the units of the army and the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you command that exercise, or operation, whatever we call it?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The exercise is commanded by a team of specialists from various branches, and at the helm of the entire operation is the person in charge of the Military Academy, which is what I was for four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: During your service at the academy, did you, as students, have cadets from other regions or of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not the cadets, but we did have such officers at higher instances of education, such as the Command Staff School, and the General Staff School. We had officers from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they usually came in teams, comprising one Serb and one Muslim. And it was less than ten years after the Dayton Accords. We had an American officer, a Chinese --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I have lost track of where we are going with all of this. I think it is -- I think it is pertinent that you turn to the issues in the witness's report that are relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was merely trying to discuss the witness's experience. I am ready to close this topic. This was actually the last question. I will move onto the report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, if you're doing that now, we're so near to the break we may as well -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we discussed your war path and wartime duties extensively. I'd like to focus on your report now. When providing your arguments, you included them in your report, and I'd briefly like to go through them, in order for you to clarify something. In paragraph 2, you described the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and you said that the armed formations, that is, the army, the TO, et cetera, at the beginning of the war, did not have full concepts and doctrine for combat operations and did not have the necessary legal framework and regulations in the area of defence. What was the concept of armed struggle? How was it defined in the former Yugoslavia, and was an attack expected to come from? What was the concept of country defence based on?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the basic concept of All People's Defence, which was in place in the then-state, was based on the idea, including theory and practice, of having an armed population as a whole. I believe such a concept, such a school of thought, missed the target basically, because weapons were distributed in local communes, companies, and other entities making part of the TO. Basically the whole idea and the doctrine was aimed at opposing an external enemy, an enemy who would come from outside. That is why all the textbooks were full of terms such as co-operation, co-ordinated action, et cetera, because it was widely believed that all forces in such circumstances ought to unite against a single foreign enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, let us go to your notes on methodology; namely, paragraphs 12 and 13. In paragraph 13, you provide your analysis about the documents and regulations, about the JNA, the SFRY in general, and the armed forces of the RS, its police and army. According to the JNA concept and the concept of the RS, in 1992, was the MUP, or -- that is to say, the police, part of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No. At that time the Ministry of Interior and its members were not part and parcel of the armed forces of the RS or what, at the time, was called the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 13, you state that when drafting this report, you relied on some other expert reports used in certain cases before this Tribunal. For the needs of the Popovic, et al. Defence, you also provided a report about the role of the morale officer in the Main Staff. When drafting this report, did you rely on the report I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I used parts of that report, because it was my report, after all. I used the introductory part, to be more specific, for practical reasons. Because I believe you acquainted me with the core of these proceedings at a rather late stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree. Our decision to call you as an expert witness came quite late in the proceedings. Tell me this, General: In paragraph 14, which is under the title: General Framework, you discuss the participants in the conflict. And you refer to paramilitary and para-police units when you explained your positions and the sides participating in the war in the former Yugoslavia, you touched upon it briefly. Can you tell us now in more detail what do you believe or how do you define these paramilitary and para-police units?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As we all know, in the fist part of 1992, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been formed. I believe it was on the 15th of April, 1992. The Croatian Defence Council had been created in late 1991, I believe. The Army of Republika Srpska, or the Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was created on the 12th of May, 1992. All those newly formed armed forces were accompanied by a number of different paramilitary and para-police forces, and I could see that for myself in Slovenia and in Croatia, because I was occasionally stopped by members of such formations, asked for an ID, and they usually just sported a hat or a military shirt; whereas, the rest would be running shoes and ordinary civilian pants. These were not parts of standard uniform, and I considered all of them to be members of such paramilitary and para-police forces.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 17, General. There, you discuss the area related to this case. Save for some specific documents pertaining to the area, did you also rely on some documents which referred to Republika Srpska in general?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I focussed on the area itself because of the nature of the indictment. This is the area stipulated in the indictment. However, I did rely on documents from the rest of Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina as I was drafting the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, let us now move to paragraph 18 in chapter 2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 18 in chapter 2, you cite the Law on All People's Defence, specifically Article 94. When we met earlier, you said that there was a typo. Could you please explain now.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's a mistake I made. Instead of Article 94, the proper reference should have been Articles 91 and 92 of the same law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the introductory part you deal with the organisation and the tasks of the armed forces of SFRY. You also provided a rather broad reference with regard to the armed forces of the SFRY. Can you explain your reason for doing so? The regulations, the doctrine, and the practice of the SFRY, were they used in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or, more specifically, in the practice of the army of the RS?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I stated in the previous section, all warring parties lacked authentic documents, legal documents above all, so they relied on what was in existence in the JNA. Certainly they all chose what suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were drafting paragraph 22, did you have methodological problems with drawing certain conclusions?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have major problems when I drafted this report. The reasons are the following: I understood that the basic topic is the use of the police, or the milicija, in combat activities. And such a thing was not provided for; it wasn't elaborated. There was only one article in the Law on All People's Defence, and that is Article 104, which I cite here, which simply states that the police can be used for combat activities. That is the only reference to the police. That is why it was a major problem to explain this matter and shed more light on it because in no country is the police meant to, or trained for, the carrying out of combat activities. That is exactly why there is such a thing as the Military Academy; whereas police officers are trained in police academies. They are trained to do something else altogether. However, in a war, there are situations that are absent from theory. Even when such situations arise and police are used for combat activities, they are always subordinated to the military officer in charge of those combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, please go to paragraphs 41 and 42. In the previous paragraphs, you included detailed, graphic representations of the commands of various types; whereas, in paragraphs 41 and 42, you deal with the setting up of temporary formations. You say there that they are tactical or operative groups of varying strength that are set up for the carrying out of temporary tasks in order to reinforce other units, or for tasks for which existing -- the existing units in the establishment are not appropriate or suitable. As for the doctrinal rules of the JNA, were such temporary formations also present in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And there are various reasons for that. Here, too, as in other wars, some other wars, at the beginning, you have a standard establishment, and during the war there's no time to set up a different one. That is why in the former JNA it was possible - and much of that was also the practice in the RS, as well as in other military formations - to set up temporary formations. Even in some of their documents, I think I found tactical groups at the level of brigade commands which can be seen as a reflection in practice of what is envisaged in theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm about to show you a document now, 2D00133. That is tab 97 in the Zupljanin Defence binder. I apologise to the interpreters that I would speak more slowly when I mention numbers. So the reference is 2D00133. I have a hard copy for you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please hand this to the witness. I see that it's upside down. It's the same in my version too. We should rotate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look at this title, or, rather, the letterhead. It says: Brigade Group Command, Skender Vakuf. And the date is 16 July 1992. Please take a look at the last page as well. You will see that, in the signature block, there is a Lieutenant-Colonel Bosko Peulic, Commander. What you spoke about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just see the last page of the original in e-court, please, for the parties to be able to see. I apologise. I actually meant the last-but-one page. The last one contains only a stamp. 00820704 is the ERN, as 15 -- as page 15 in e-court. Now we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, is this what you were explaining, a temporary formation?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It can be interpreted that way. For certain reasons, probably a larger combat formation was to be set up because of the needs on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, sir, who was able to issue the order to set up this group of brigades and appoint its commander?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please switch off the microphone when not in use.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the superior commander, always. I suppose that if Peulic is the commander, that he had the approval or the order of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take at look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN 00820692 is the page I would like to see now. And that is page 3 of the Serbian version in e-court; whereas, it's page 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here, you can see of what that group of brigades consists. The 122nd Light Infantry Brigade, the Skender Vakuf Light Brigade, and the Kotor Varos Light Brigade. General, we see that the title is: Tasks of Subordinate Units. Can we see who those units are and who their commander is?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see that heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please go to 97 in your binder and then move to page 2. Can you see item 2? That's the group of brigades.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: And item 5 contains the tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But in item 2, we see the brigades that make up the group of brigades. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And on the following page you will see the task of the subordinate units. Then you will see which units these are. Under 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
