utterances.text: Which units are subordinate to the group of brigades and the group commander, Peulic? Can you see?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's the very units that are listed under item 2. These are the units to which he issues orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic didn't only command his own unit but also all these?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And under 5.3, where the tasks of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade are listed, and it's on page 4 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 5.3, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on page 7 of the Serbian version in e-court, Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic says that the command post of the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade should be at the public security station of Kotor Varos. Was it usual practice, sir, that the brigade headquarters should be at -- or on the premises of the -- of a public security station? And what does that mean for the functioning of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this, indeed, is very unusual practice. I don't believe that no other suitable premises could be found to accommodate the command post of this group of brigades. The functioning of the public security station was made impossible by this decision.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before Mr. Krgovic moves on, perhaps we could hear from the General how he knows that the functioning of the public security station was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't ask the witness if he knows anything about the functioning but how that affects the functioning. That was the essence of my question. Under the circumstances, what was the position of the people there and what was their relationship with the military command? That was the gist of my question, rather than whether the police station functioned or not. And I tried to elicit an answer based on this order and military doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm so sorry, but the actual question was - and I perhaps should have objected at that stage: What does that mean for the functioning of the public security station. That's page 51, line 8, and in fact the General answered it by saying: "The functioning of the public security station was made impossible by this decision," or "but this decision." And I'm asking the basis for which the General is able to give this opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], General, can you please answer this question.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I know what a command post looks like, a command post of one brigade. Here we're talking about a group of brigades. I know how much space is required and what kind of working conditions. A small public security station, such as this one, certainly didn't have enough space for so many people. And it is also unusual for a command post to be at a public security station. Because if you place it there, you subordinate the station to yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, General, by establishing the brigade's headquarters in the public security station, that station would become a lawful military target, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let's go back to your report. Take another look at paragraphs 41 and 42. When you speak about temporary formations, what about the rules of commanding, such as singleness of command and unity of command? Would they also apply to these temporary formations, as well as to establishment units?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Wherever an army is commanded, it is exclusively founded on the principles of singleness of command and subordination. It is very clear who the commander is and who the subordinates are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Even if the commanders of those brigades have the same rank and the same kind of position as Mr. Peulic, so that the rules of rank and position are disregarded?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The basic relationship in the army is that of superior officer and subordinate. And there is a hierarchical relationship, talking about ranks. In this case, though, the commander of a group of brigades, irrespective of the ranks of the commanders of the individual brigades, is the highest-ranking officer, and all commanders of the other brigades are subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I just have another question. I forgot about this aspect. When the mission is accomplished or when there's no more need for such a temporary formation, every brigade continues to execute its tasks as part of the regular establishment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is a decision about the -- setting-up of the group of brigades, and it is set up to carry out certain tasks. Once they are carried out and when there's no need for its further existence, a decision about its dissolution should be taken, and the manpower, as well as the materiel and equipment, are returned to their previous units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The reasons for setting up such a temporary formation can be to take a town, say, or reach certain positions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Usually in the preamble of the decision the reasons for setting it up are stated. It can be the defence of a town or another populated place. Or reaching a certain line or carrying out certain stages of an operation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The execution of this order and taking certain positions and so on, can these be termed combat tasks?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Such a temporary formation is exclusively set up to carry out some combat operations. This is a substantial force; three brigades, after all. They wouldn't have been set up to carry out peacetime operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, please go to the part of your report which has to do with formation, organisation, and tasks of the armed forces of Republika Srpska, paragraphs 43 and onwards. I'm looking specifically at the paragraphs 43 to 48 or 49. Save for the constitutional law that you refer to, there are no other footnotes or references. Did you base this specific part of your report on your personal experience?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an important part. Why there are no footnotes for some of these assertions should not be led. It should be asked in a non-leading form as to what this is based on, because that's obviously important. And the same follows for any other questions along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you wish me to do so I can go paragraph at a time. I was trying to cut the time short and I may have been a bit clumsy in the way I formulated my question. I simply wanted to ask the General about the footnotes on page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What were your sources save for the constitutional law on the proclamation? What else did you rely on as a source?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Should I begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krgovic, I take it that's page 14 in the Serbian version of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the English version, please bear with me. Page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: When drafting this part of the report, I relied on my own experience. I occasionally presented similar arguments when I visited the units in the field. I was a participant in those events. And I also shot documentaries about this topic. That is why I believed no footnotes were necessary, save for the one I did include.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you formulated these conclusions, were you aware that there's a different view of the breakup of Yugoslavia and a different interpretation of the events in question; namely, on the Croatian and Muslim side. To what extent could you be objective in presenting your position?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't analyse their positions in my report. There was no time, and I believe I said already what was the basis for my position. What I knew was the information we were provided with. The JNA had these as its official tasks, and it was engaged in preventing armed interethnic conflict, as I said in para 46. I do know that there was a hostile sentiment at the time in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was held not only by the Croatian and Muslim population but also by certain individuals in the Serb -- Serbian public, and I specified a few such examples, as you can see in paragraph 46. I was familiar with the propaganda campaign underway at the time. You mention in the first part of my presentation that I was in charge of a press centre located in the town of Bihac in the army hall. One of my tasks then was to collect all media reports, together with my team, and to forward it to my superior command. I am very well acquainted with the content of such media reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 45, at the beginning, you say that it was obvious that the Muslim-Croat part of the BH leadership wanted to declare independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina without the agreement of the representatives of the Serbian people. Was it, indeed, done in that way?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As regards paragraph 46, was there any propaganda put forth by the Bosnian leadership, in terms of any recruits responding to military call-ups?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I believe I discussed it a moment ago. I said that it was a daily occurrence. I followed it when I was at the helm of the press centre. I collated such information and forwarded it to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, you also said that you, at a certain point in time, were in charge of personnel affairs. When it comes to JNA officers and soldiers, what was your role in that regard? Once they left the force, did you issue them with certificates and were you in charge of the administrative side of things?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In such cases when they left voluntarily. They first had to submit an application, a request, following which the necessary documentation was issued to them. I even went so far as to conduct -- or have a conversation with each and every one, especially the officers, in a friendly manner. Frequently, I saw people leave who were part of my class at school. There were some difficult situations in such circumstances as well, and difficult cases, because people came from mixed marriages or had spouses of different ethnicities, and they simply asked for my support and advice. In such situations, I proposed individual solutions to the best of my knowledge and ability. I thought such solutions were the best option for the people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As you state in the last sentence of paragraph 46, were there any cases in which military conscripts took their equipment and personal arms with them?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Such instances existed across the territory of Yugoslavia from Slovenia, to Bosnia, and further on. Once they deserted their units, they usually take -- took their equipment and weapons. Many of our warehouses, especially those storing live ammunition and weapons, were blocked. Usually such warehouses were manned by only two or three people, and, as such, were easily overrun by TO forces. In this way, such TOs could gain access to those supplies. We know of the case of Major Tepic who blew up not only his warehouse but himself too, rather than to see it fall into the hands of the enemy. But these were individual, isolated cases. In such isolated warehouses, there was also personnel who came from specific ethnic groups, such as Slovenes and Croats, and that made things easier for their TOs. Our entire radar equipment remained in Bjelovar, which is a garrison near Zagreb in Croatia. It is also well-known that pilots deserted and took away their helicopters and jet planes, although there weren't too many such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, can I just kick in a question here, because it wasn't quite clear to me who were blocking these warehouses. Did you mean to say, if I understood you correctly, that whichever TO had the upper hand in the vicinity of the TO -- of the warehouse, would seize control of the warehouse? Or was the warehouse, or the warehouses, in general, protected by the JNA or ... What was the situation? Who actually blocked and guarded these warehouses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, such warehouses were the property of the JNA and were guarded by JNA members. Such facilities were blocked by the paramilitary formations of Slovenia, Croatia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, for as long as the JNA was the official armed force, and until those republics declared their independence. However, as JNA members, there were officers or soldiers in those warehouses of different ethnicities, and if they were in the majority, such facilities were handed over without any fight, without struggle. Or, in other cases, they fled, abandoned their warehouse, leaving mostly Serb soldiers behind. I'm not saying that this was done by all officers and soldiers of Croatian, Muslim, or Slovenian ethnicity. There were a few of them, who, irrespective of the conflicts and calls from their respective republics, chose to stay with the JNA. For the most part, such people remained in the Republic of Serbia because they no longer dared return to their republics because of that deed. In some cases, there -- even their civil rights and rights as citizens were taken away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure we will get to the bottom of this. Please proceed, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in addition to your immediate and direct experience in Bihac and the area, did you have occasion to communicate with some other JNA formations, say, in Sarajevo or Tuzla? Did they experience similar tendencies, or is this -- is what you describe limited to Bihac?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm sorry, I didn't understand him to be talking about Bihac. I understand him to be talking about Slovenia and Croatia. So I don't know where the Bihac business comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I began this line of questioning with Bihac. The witness said that it all took place from Slovenia, to Croatia, to Bosnia-Herzegovina, following the same scenario. And that was my initial question. The witness did expand and touch upon certain events in Slovenia and Croatia, but the gist of my question was Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I believe we understand each other. Could you please explain to the Chamber what it is that you were trying to explain about the sieges and departure of soldiers. Does this pertain to Slovenia and Croatia, as well as Bihac, or did you have something specific in mind?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I started off with Slovenia, but it also applies to Bosnia and Herzegovina. As you said, the scenario was the same or similar. A civil war, in theory, focuses on demolishing the existing state structure and organisation, including the existing armed force, which, in this case, was the JNA, and the state in question used to be called the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. By destroying that state and its armed forces, you, in parallel, create your own military organisation. The process followed in parallel, following the same scenario, with a lot of bloodshed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, let me go back to my original question before Ms. Korner objected. Were you in contact with other military structures and JNA units in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did you exchange information with them and did they encounter similar situations?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The focus of my work was to inform the servicemen about all current events. What was the basis of my focus? First of all, each unit, say, at the level of regiment, discussed the news. That is to say, how many people fled, how many people were killed, how many people took away weapons, and you have it funneled through the system of command and subordination to the superior command and this all went up to what, at the time, was still called the Federal Secretariat for All People's Defence. That was the central organ receiving all the information in the evening, producing a summary or an overview of events which would then be distributed to all the units in question the next day. Then I would take that and inform others. We knew for that reason what was happening in Tuzla, in Bihac, in Mostar, Sarajevo, et cetera, when it comes to these topics. [In English] Please, water. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, let us now go back to your report. In paragraph 48, well, paragraph 47 seems to include some general facts. But in paragraph 48, you say that units and staffs of Territorial Defence manned mostly by Muslims were incorporated into the BH army. And those manned mostly by Croats into the Croatian Defence Council. Further on, you say that former JNA officers chose where to go based on their ethnicity. Were you able to see it for yourself through contacts with your colleagues during and before the war? Did you stay in touch with any of your Muslim, Croat, and other officers; and do you know what their fate was?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: After the war, as the head of the Military Academy, I had a chance to travel to Slovenia and to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Sarajevo. Of course, ten years after the war, we discussed all topics. It is in this way that I gained an impression of what they went through. There seems to be something that I may have omitted in the report, and that is to include that the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, by virtue of its decision of the 8th of April, abolished the existing republican TO staff which was mixed, in terms of ethnic composition, and was still part of the old concept of the Yugoslav national TO. Instead, they established their republican TO staff with predominantly Muslims. Following that decision, later in April, I believe, they issued another, declaring an immediate threat of war, and I believe that by the 15th of April, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established. When I was commander of the Military Academy, a military attaché and the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Belgrade invited me to their receptions in order to celebrate that day when they formed their armed forces. And I went, gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, let us go to paragraph 50 of your report. There, you say that when the SFRY Presidency adopted a decision on the withdrawal of the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbian political leadership in Bosnia-Herzegovina set out to form its army in the area where the Serbs were in the majority because Muslim and Croatian armies had already been formed. You are actually referring to the dates you mentioned a moment ago. That is to say, the 15th of April, 1992, and the formation of the HVO in 1991, if I am not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. I overheard Ms. Korner's question. It was a leading question, but I'm trying to speed things up. It was just a technical question, and it is not anything new. I'm simply doing this in order to cut time short.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps when the General's finished for the day I can just mention why I'm taking these objections, in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And just for -- for clarification, General, you seem to indicate in paragraph 45 that the VRS - or am I wrong? - was established sometime in January 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm not saying that the army was established but, rather, that the Republika Srpska was proclaimed, and the army - that is, the VRS - was only established on 12 May 1992. That's what my report says, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's correct. I just saw that in paragraph 52. Please forgive me. And proceed, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, in paragraph 51 of your report, you mention the amendments to the constitution when you discuss the legal foundation and the laws and regulations governing the establishment of the VRS. When you compared the decisions on this establishment, were they in line with the decisions of the highest legislative body of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. First, the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established; that was its name at the time. I think that only in August 1992 its name changed to Republika Srpska. First, the assembly was constituted and then the Speaker of the assembly, then the president of the republic. There was a cabinet, and only then were ministries set up, and eventually the VRS, the army. That is first and foremost because the RS, or the Serbian Republic of BiH, until the end, officially supported the JNA and expressed its wish, and only as a -- its wish that, even as a constituted entity, to remain part of Yugoslav. Even then they didn't decide to establish their own army until the Federation decided to withdraw the Yugoslav People's Army as the federal army from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And, as you see, the decision on the withdrawal of the JNA was adopted on the 4th of May and it was to remain in force until the 19th of May; whereas, the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was set up on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, you said that, if I understood you correctly, on the 10th of May you left Bosnia-Herzegovina. What was the decision with regard to officers who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who hailed from there? What was the Presidency's decision with regard to their status?

utterances.speaker: VIDOSAV KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot exactly remember the decision, but I know that there was the suggestion that all officers, non-commissioned officers and soldiers of the former JNA, who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina or who hailed from there, that they should remain in the VRS. But I believe that this was not an order; that it was left to them to decide themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it is almost the time, so I'll go to next topic, so I think we can finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: General we're about to take the adjournment for the day. You, having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side until you're released by the Trial Chamber, and, indeed, in such conversations as you have with persons other than counsel, you can't discuss your testimony. That is something that I would ask you to bear in mind each time we take a day's adjournment and I would probably repeat it on -- on the weekend for reinforcement. But we take the adjournment to reconvene in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I ask the General leave first and can I just very briefly address Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, the usher will please escort ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's just this. There is an issue in this case about the General's report, his sources and how he comes to the conclusions that he does. And therefore I would ask that no leading questions are asked about how he has come to the opinion or asserted the fact that he has asserted in the various paragraphs. It's as simple as that. It can be done in non-leading form: What did you mean, where did you go this information from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So Mr. Krgovic will govern himself accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that. There is -- because I'm trying to formulate question in that way because of the objection that Ms. Korner who said that where is the paragraph based on his own experience and I quoted the paragraph and start reading the paragraph, so that's why. But I will take care about that, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
